About one person in
ten is left-handed,
and that ratio seems
to be older than
our own species.
So here is the puzzle.
If sharing the same
hand makes life easier,
why didn't left-handers
simply disappear?
One possible answer starts
with a fight.
First, why would most
people favor one side at all?
One answer is cooperation.
Our ancestors lived in
close-knit groups that
shared tools, weapons and
skills.
If most people used
the same hand,
a tool made by
one person fit everyone
else, and a child
could copy an adult's
movements without flipping
them around.
In 2012, Daniel Abrams
and Mark Panaggio built
a mathematical model of
this idea.
If cooperation were the
only force, left-handedness
would slowly disappear.
But their model also
includes a second force
pulling the other way:
competition.
The balance between the
two can produce a
steady minority of
left-handers.
Picture a fight between
two ancient warriors.
Most fighters spent their
lives facing right-handed
opponents, and their
reflexes were tuned to
blows from familiar angles.
A left-handed opponent
changes everything.
The strikes come from
the other side,
and the timing feels wrong.
This is called the
fighting hypothesis.
Biologists call this
negative frequency-dependent
selection.
A trait is valuable
precisely because it is rare.
If left-handers became
common, everyone would
train against them,
and the surprise would vanish.
So the advantage shrinks
as their numbers grow,
and the trait can
never take over.
Is there any evidence?
In 2005, the French
researchers Charlotte Faurie
and Michel Raymond compared
traditional societies.
Among the Dioula of
Burkina Faso, where homicide
was very rare,
about three point four
percent were left-handed.
Among the Eipo of
New Guinea, where violence
was common, about
twenty-seven percent.
It's a correlation, not proof.
You can still see
the edge today,
in sports where you
face an opponent.
In boxing and mixed
martial arts, left-handed
fighters, often called
southpaws, are more common
than their ten percent
share would predict.
In swimming or running,
they have no special
advantage.
The edge exists only
when someone is trying
to read your moves.
So cooperation pulls us
toward one side,
and competition keeps a
small left-handed group alive.
About ten percent may
be where those two
forces balance.
The full story,
from cave walls to
twin studies, is on
Miya's Lab.
